title: Coupled Training with Privileged Information and Unlabeled Data
topic: General Machine Learning->Unsupervised and Semi-supervised Learning
claim: Whether using extra training-only information helps depends on its signal strength: a strong signal gives gains, while a weak one gives gains only at a tuned constraint.
layout: 2 side-by-side line plots, shared y-label, red dashed baseline and star marking best value
description: Two side-by-side line plots share the y-axis label 'Test MSE', and the x-axis is the constraint value ν. Each plot has a blue dotted curve for Coupled Training. A red dashed horizontal line marks the baseline, OLS on X only. A red star marks the best ν. Panel (a), 'Strong privileged signal (large ||θ||2)', shows a curve that rises almost linearly from the star at the left, where MSE is lowest at about 2.78. It then reaches the baseline at about 3.13 and flattens. Panel (b), 'Weak privileged signal (small ||θ||2)', shows MSE dropping steeply from about 2.8 at small ν to a shallow minimum of about 1.74 near ν=127. It then climbs back to the baseline at about 1.99 and flattens. The legends are boxed, and the captions are italic under each panel.
caption: Linear Gaussian signal strength. Performance of the proposed method under varying levels of privileged signal strength.
abstract: In many prediction problems, we have extra information during training (for example, measurements that are expensive or slow to collect) that will not be available when the model is deployed. A common strategy is to first train a model that uses all training information, then use its predictions on unlabeled examples to train a second model that only uses the inputs available at test time. However, when the extra training-only information is weak or noisy, this Two-Stage approach can mislead the deployment model and even hurt accuracy. We propose a joint training method that learns the two models together, so the deployment model can benefit from the extra information only when it actually helps, instead of inheriting its mistakes. We provide guarantees that describe when joint training improves prediction accuracy and analyze a simple alternating training algorithm for large, high-dimensional models. Experiments on synthetic data and real-world prediction tasks show that our approach avoids these failures and robustly outperforms standard Two-Stage baselines.
